title: Utility Function
body:
$U(s)$: a number saying how much a [[Rational Agent]] prefers state $s$. It turns "I would rather
have this than that" into arithmetic, which is the only reason an agent can compare options it has
never seen together.

## Why a preference ordering is not enough

An agent could just rank outcomes: $A \succ B \succ C$. That is sufficient when outcomes are
certain, and it collapses the moment they are not. Ranking cannot answer "is a 50% chance of $A$
better than $B$ for sure?", because that question is about **how much** better $A$ is than $B$,
and an ordering has no how-much.

Numbers answer it. That is the whole argument for utilities, and it is why this note exists
before [[Expected Utility]] rather than inside it.

The von Neumann-Morgenstern result makes it respectable: **if an agent's preferences satisfy a
handful of common-sense axioms** (transitivity, and that if $A \succ B \succ C$ then some lottery
between $A$ and $C$ is exactly as good as $B$), **then a utility function exists whose expectation
the agent is maximising**, and it is unique up to positive linear rescaling. So the choice is not
"use utilities or not"; it is "have coherent preferences or not". An agent with intransitive
preferences ($A \succ B \succ C \succ A$) can be charged a fee to go round the loop forever.

**Scale is arbitrary.** $U$ and $2U + 7$ describe the same agent. Utilities are meaningful in
comparison, never in isolation, and a single utility number on its own says nothing at all.

## Utility is not money

The classic demonstration: a certain \$1,000,000, against a coin flip for \$3,000,000 or nothing.
The expected *money* favours the flip (\$1.5M against \$1M) and almost everyone takes the certain
million, correctly. Utility is **concave** in money: the second million is worth less than the
first, so the flip's expected utility is lower even though its expected dollars are higher.

That concavity **is** risk aversion, and the whole point is that it needs no separate mechanism.
An agent maximising expected utility on a concave $U$ is risk-averse automatically. A linear $U$
is risk-neutral, and a convex one buys lottery tickets.

## Several objectives at once

Real decisions trade off things that do not share a unit: a route that is fast, cheap, and safe;
a design that is light, strong, and manufacturable. **Multi-attribute utility** handles it by
combining the attributes into one number, usually as a weighted sum:

$$U(s) = w_1 x_1(s) + w_2 x_2(s) + \cdots + w_n x_n(s)$$

Two things worth knowing about that formula:

- **The weights are where the value judgements hide.** They are not discovered from data; someone
  chose them, and choosing them *is* the decision about what the system cares about. Changing a
  weight changes what the agent does far more visibly than changing the algorithm.
- Sometimes no trade-off is needed. If option $A$ beats $B$ on every attribute, $A$ **dominates**
  and you can discard $B$ without knowing the weights at all. Doing that first usually removes
  most of the candidates.

The same weighted-sum shape appears as [[Weights]] in a [[Neural Network]] and as the objective in
[[Optimization]]. It is the standard move for reducing many numbers to one, and it has the
standard weakness: the sum can hide a catastrophic value in one attribute behind good values in
the others.
